ab_banff_national_park.blurb: Banff National Park lies in Alberta's Rockies beside the Trans-Canada Highway, and climbing here spans crag sport routes, alpine peaks and some of the best known ice in the country. Sport dominates the roped routes, mostly 5.9 to 5.12 and centred on 5.10, with a smaller trad scene, and winter adds ice from WI3 to WI7 and some mixed routes. The rock is a mix: quartzite at Lake Louise is the park's best, Tunnel Mountain offers quartzite and limestone, and rock elsewhere in the Rockies can be poor. Crags start to dry out as early as May, and ice season runs from about mid-November into spring. Sunshine Rock and Radium Highway are other main sport areas.

ct_eastern_coastal_slope.blurb: This stretch of Connecticut's shoreline lowlands is mostly a bouldering region, with a smaller amount of trad and a few sport and top-rope climbs. Many boulders sit on slopes above swamps or ponds, left behind by glaciers. Grades run from V0 to V5 for most of them, with a tail of hard problems up to V12. The rock varies: the Westwoods boulders are coarse granite, and fine grey gneiss is found across the state's southeast. Many of the problems are tucked away in woods, so exploring is part of it. Main pockets are Mystic, Westwoods, Killingworth and Chatfield Hollow.

az_granite_dells.blurb: The Granite Dells are a maze of rounded granite domes and boulders just north and east of Prescott, with Watson Lake tucked among them. The rock is medium-grained desert granite that can feel a bit grainy on some formations, and it weathered along its joints into the lumpy shapes seen today. Trad makes up most of the climbing, with a good helping of sport and a few top-ropes and boulders. Roped grades run mostly from 5.7 to 5.11 and peak at 5.10, so moderates are plentiful. Development keeps going, particularly around Watson Lake. The biggest sections are the crags along the Peavine Trail, Granite Gardens and Watson Lake.

bc_vancouver_island.blurb: Vancouver Island pairs coastal scenery with a wide mix of rock, so quality is uneven. Most of the island is basalt, with sandstone and conglomerate around Nanaimo, limestone in patches and granite in the north. Sport climbing leads, and there is a good deal of trad plus a bit of top-rope and bouldering. Roped grades run mostly from 5.8 to 5.12, centred on 5.10 and 5.11, with a few harder lines above. Some limestone venues are steep and overhanging. Beyond the crags, glaciated peaks and remote alpine terrain are found in the island's mountains. The biggest areas are Comox Lake, Victoria, Quadra Island and Strathcona Provincial Park.

ca_castle_rock_area.blurb: This area sits in the Santa Cruz Mountains south of San Jose, and it is mostly a bouldering destination. The sandstone is sculpted into bulbous shapes, and the problems lean toward slopers and mantles on smooth rock with few footholds. Bouldering grades run from V0 to V5 for most, with a thin tail up to V12. A smaller set of crags adds sport and top-rope climbing, mostly in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, at places such as Summit Rock and Indian Rock. Sandstone breaks easily when wet, so give it a few days after rain. The main season runs from late October through April, before heat and mosquitoes set in.

nm_organ_mountains.blurb: The Organ Mountains rise just east of Las Cruces on the edge of the Chihuahuan Desert. Granite makes up the northern part of the range, rhyolite lies in the middle, and the low southern end is limestone, with climbing mostly in the north. Trad leads, with bouldering nearly as common, and a bit of top-rope and sport. Roped grades run mostly from 5.6 to 5.11, with a broad middle around 5.8 to 5.10, while problems are mostly V0 to V4. Approaches over hot desert are long and the range stays quiet. Some walls give sunny winter cragging and others stay shady in summer. Key sections include Aguirre Bouldering, Rabbit Ears, the South Organs and the High Horns.
